final_message:
I've built the workbook with all the requested tabs. One serious problem came up: every one of the 39 stores has exactly the same figures, so the store view can't be used to compare stores. Also, I couldn't open the file in Excel to confirm the PivotTables load cleanly.

**Data problem:** each store's rows are an exact copy of Store 1's, so Sales by Store shows the same brand mix 39 times and each store total is 1/39 of the chain. This looks like an error in the extract. Ranking stores or moving stock based on that tab would be misleading until you get a corrected store-level extract. Brand-level ST% and mix are not affected by this.

**What's in the workbook:**
- **Data:** your original sheet, renamed. The figures are unchanged; I only added a filter and a frozen header row.
- **Sales by Brand:** a PivotTable of brand totals with your 13 column headers and a Grand Total row.
- **Sales by Store:** a PivotTable with Store and Brand Name, a total row for each store, a Grand Total row, and your 14 headers. Stores are listed 1 to 39 rather than alphabetically, which would put Store 10 before Store 2.
- **Both tabs also have a formula version of the same table**, starting in column P, with the same headers and totals. It updates without a refresh and should match the PivotTable exactly. I added it because of the Excel issue below.
- **Notes:** a short tab with the data alert, my assumptions, a set of check figures, and some first read-outs.

**Excel check:** both PivotTables are set to refresh when the file opens. When I tried to open a test copy, Excel was already running on your Mac (open about 22 hours) and stopped responding, probably on a dialog. I didn't touch that window, so check whether a prompt is waiting on your screen. If the PivotTables come up empty, use Data > Refresh All. The formula tables work either way, and I checked their values against totals worked out directly from the data.

**Decisions you should check:**
- **ST% is units sold ÷ units on hand.** Stock on hand is a unit count, so I didn't divide dollars by it. Totals are summed sales over summed stock, not an average of percentages.
- **ST% can go above 100%** with this formula. For example, Shiseido's MTD is 168%.
- **The file gives a separate stock-on-hand figure for WTD, MTD and YTD** and doesn't say how each one is measured. I used each as given; worth confirming before acting on the ratios.

**Other data issues (all listed in Notes):**
- The extract's own "Sell Through %" column doesn't match your formula, so I didn't use it.
- Sales $ doesn't equal units × retail price on any row.
- Some products have the wrong category.
- There is no week-ending date in the file.

**Headline numbers:** WTD ST% for the department is 25.1%, MTD is 81.1% and YTD is 72.4%. Clinique (48.6%) and Kiehl's (56.4%) have the lowest YTD ST% and the most stock on hand, so they're worth a look for cutting orders or promotions. Elizabeth Arden is at 101% YTD, which suggests a risk of running out.

DONE

Files are in outputs/:
- Weekly Sales Data - Pivot Analysis.xlsx
